newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss 1997 budget passes first parliament hurdle.
newsitem.headline: Swiss 1997 budget passes first parliament hurdle.

text.p: Switzerland's lower house of parliament on Thursday passed a draft federal budget for 1997 with a deficit of 5.7 billion Swiss francs despite cost cutting to keep spending barely higher than 1996 levels.

The spending plan must still pass by the upper chamber and will most likely go back to a joint committee of both houses to iron out differing details before it can be adopted as scheduled by mid-December.
The vote of 89 to 37 in favour with 32 abstaining approved expenditures of 44.5 billion Swiss francs, as against projected spending this year of 44.0 billion.
The 1996 deficit is budgeted at 4.05 billion but Berne has said nine-month data indicated the actual gap could be 500 million to one billion francs wider.
Parliament also approved a measure empowering the cabinet to borrow about 500 million Swiss francs for additional spending it can release during the year if Swiss economioc growth is too slow.

The 1997 budget is based on government projections of 1.5 percent real economic growth and the deficit could swell as high as seven billion if the economy remains stagnant next year, Finance Minister Kaspar Villiger said last month.

The government forecast for the economy, which has contracted for six consecutive quarters, is at the high end of analysts' expectations that have turned increasingly bearish in light of the Swiss franc's persistent strength and structural problems.
The Swiss National Bank sees gross domestic product rising 1.0 to 1.5 percent next year after shrinking an expected 0.5 percent in 1996. GDP rose a measly 0.1 percent in 1995.

Swiss bonds shrugged off the budget proposal, which does not have the same impact in Switzerland as in other major industrialised countries because of the relatively large importance of finance at the cantonal and local community level. -- Zurich Newsroom, +41-1-631 7340
